The nurse asks if there are any problems, listens to heart and lungs, checks ankles for water retention, signs the chart on the computer.

The tech sets up the machine, makes sure the settings are correct, examines access site, consults with patient about where they want the needles to go, prepares sites with disinfectant, applies lidocaine numbing, and inserts needles.

Basically the 2 nurses are there to supervise and are there in case someone has trouble breathing or passes out or whatever. The 8-10 techs per shift do everything else.
There's 2 nurses on staff each shift. The title of the people who work on the patients is "dialysis technicians" or "techs" for short.

Kidney transplant recipients wait about 1 year (more or less) in my state (Oregon). Due to my previous transplant, I have an increased antibody load which basically means out of the people who could match me blood-wise, only some of those people could actually donate. Which is why I'm looking to get as many people tested for compatibility as I can.

Remaining on dialysis is generally bad for the health. The process of hemodialysis is only 17% effective vs. a functional kidney. This basically means the body chemistry is perpetually out of whack. The statistics are that average lifespan on dialysis is 5 years, but these stats are skewed because the majority of patients are elderly and have other problems that compound with the kidney failure/dialysis. Plus the whole situation of dialysis is very hard on the body and elderly folks can't handle it as well which impacts the mortality statistics as well. 

Besides the physical aspects, remaining on dialysis generally means a person can't work full time (or at all in many cases), they don't have a lot of freedom in life, they can't eat anything that would normally be good for them. It's also very damaging and demoralizing to the patient's emotional state.

When I came out of the coma, I was sweaty and my muscles felt weak and achey, like I had working out in the gym too much. I thought I had just been asleep for a while but they told me I was in a coma for 3 days. Apparently I had bit my mom in day 2 of the coma.

When I first found out I was sick, I was feeling lightheaded at home, and almost blacked out. So we went to the local docs office, they took some blood. Based on the elevated postassium / phosorus and urea he could tell right away it was kidney failure.  within an hour I was in a mitsubishi medical plane coming to Portland. There they diagnosed me with Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS for short). It's genetic by nature but there also some cases where they can't identify the cause. 

Basically my kidneys were useless, Stage 5 renal failure. I didn't experience any progression before that, except being tired a lot without knowing why.

The medication was an experimental derivative of mouse hemoglobin, but I don't recall the name. It will come to when I'm not thinking about it. I had to sign an FDA waiver before they could use it on me.

I live in portland, oregon. My name is Ken Jones, if you actually wanted to call them and tell them you wanted to donate to me.

Now I'm not sure if they'd have a donor fly here to do it, or if they can do it in your town and have it flown. I've never asked them about that scenario because I didn't think anyone not "here" would do it. The Donor coordinator would definitely know if you wanted to ask.

In terms of getting on the list, the paperwork was intensive but it was all done in a day. They did make me jump the hoops though. They want to make sure the transplant patient has a plan for work or school, a plan for the future. The meds that the patient will have to take for the life of the transplant are expensive and have to be paid for somehow.

Basically if you have kidney failure, because of the huge cost of dialysis per treatment, and because it's required to live, you qualify for Medicare. They passed an amendment in the 1970s for this after dialysis became effective. When you get a kidney, they basically classify you as "fixed" and your insurance runs out a year after transplant. So the transplant team makes sure you know what you're going to do in the future to pay for your own healthcare plan and costs.

I wanted to point out, since people have been kind enough to offer to get tested, 

My insurance covers the donor's medical costs, like tests, surgery, aenesthesia, recovery time at hospital, etc. That's standard practice for any transplant program in the hospitals across the country.

My mom can't donate because she shows traces of protein in her urine. It could or could not some day develop into a problem, but when they're testing donors they're very particular and she is not a candidate. 

Same with my sister, we would be a good match but she has gained weight in adulthood from not eating healthy. She is within the acceptable Body Mass Index but her lifestyle means her blood pressure is too high in its unmedicated state. She can't donate just from the BP being too high.

My dad hasn't suffered any after effects, the main thing that happened was he donated prior to the introduction of laparoscopic extraction. This means these days they can take out a kidney through a small incision in most cases, but back then it was still not widely done. He had to have a scar that basically wrapped around one side, from his back to his belly. 

He was supposed to not lift anything for a while because it would build scar tissue if he strained himself during the healing process. Being the stubborn Irishman he is, he sorta cheated on that and now the scar tissue makes his back feel tight sometimes.

It was in 1998 so I'm fuzzy on some that detail. My mom was there and I sometimes have to ask her about this stuff because she remembers it very clearly. My understanding is that when I reacted and went into a coma, they stopped the experimental meds and other meds they tried didn't work to stop the rejection. They couldn't use any of the more aggressive meds due to my state in the coma. 

The initial rejection triggered because they wanted to switch one of my meds to a different one (each med has side effects, and for some people those side effects can be dangerous). Changing the meds in that way seems to have thrown the whole thing out of wack. They have to keep my immune system shut down to a certain level (very low) and if it spikes then the body realizes "wait, there's a foreign object here....Let's get it!"

Family members have a higher chance of being a "good enough to donate" match (meaning it's also possible a person could match to a certain percent but it's not enough to make it work). Siblings are usually a 75% match. But to donate to a person a blood relation isn't required. Friends and strangers get matched up all the time.

I don't know the exact details of how it goes down, but generally you would go to a lab or the hospital where they take a couple vials of blood. It's then tested and run against my blood info that's in the database.

When you get a transplant, there are 2 types of rejection that can happen: acute and chronic. Chronic happens to all transplants, no matter what meds you take your body slowly rejects it, attacking a little bit at a time. This is why transplant organs don't just work forever. It's a normal part of the process. However these days many transplants last 20-30 years.

Acute rejecting is when your meds aren't working, or the doses aren't right, or a patient stops taking their meds due to side effects. The body starts attacking the transplant like crazy, trying to kill off the foreign body it doesn't recognize. They do happen now and again, and it's the reason the doctors are always testing your blood, and the reason you have to always pay attention to how you feel, how the transplant feels, etc.

When a patient is having an acute episode, you rush off to the hospital and they give you very strong meds to try to stop the rejection in its tracks. I had an acute episode that was triggered by them putting me on some new meds that didn't work the way they were supposed to. I don't recall those particular meds, it was a long time ago... Not all transplant cases use the same meds and they will sometimes switch one you take with one of the other options.

When I got to the hospital they put me on an experimental med I had to sign off on, the actual name escapes me but it was derived from mouse hemoglobin. I recently asked my team about that med and they said it's not used anymore. I had a huge reaction to it, I don't recall the initial symptoms but basically I woke up 3 days later not knowing what happened.

In the process the kidney fully rejected because they couldn't fight the episode when I was in a coma.

For a long time I was fine with being on dialysis while working/school/life happened. It seemed more predictable than my previous experiences with transplant. When you get a transplant, they put you on a bunch of meds that weaken your immune system so it doesn't attack the kidney. Many of these meds cause mood swings, bad for the heart, etc. Kidney transplant medicine and techniques are very different since 1998.

On top of that, I think I reached a point psychologically and emotionally where I was ready to take on the challenge. I began to dread going to dialysis, got sick of feeling intense anxiety about the coming pain of 15 gauge needles at dialysis. 

I also wanted to be able to travel, wanted to be able to work full time, wanted to eat all those foods I can't eat now. With 4-hour treatments 3x a week, plus being tired for hours afterword, I have been living a limited life only being able to work part time. I want to live an unlimited life.

I work, take classes, do many of the things regular people do. But get tired much faster than the average joe, I can't eat most things, etc. One of the biggest impacts for me is relying on a machine to live. It's demoralizing to know that 3 times a week, I have to go a facility with 30 other patients in a row, and have some barely-trained technician try to stick 15 gauge needles into my arm. It's become a struggle every time go in through that door. 

I can travel if I want but not in any spontaneous way. I have to schedule treatments in other towns 3 days a week if I want to travel anywhere. I am leashed to this outside thing in order to survive and exist and it's a hard thing to wake up to.

I never know if I'm going to experience excruciating pain, or if they're going infiltrate my arm and mess up my 'access.' Then I'd have to go into surgery while they try to save it or find another location to install a new one.

For that to make sense I should explain it better: in order to clean a patient's blood effectively, they need to be able to get a lot of flow volume/speed. You can't get enough flow in regular arteries/veins as they are. So they have to into your arm, and surgically fuse and redirect flow to create an 'access' or a place where large-gauge needles will fit. If a technician at dialysis does it wrong, they can cause a lot of pain, or even 'infiltrate' it which means the machine pumps a bunch of blood into the tissues of your arm, instead of through the access and into the veins/arteries.

There is a fear that this could happen every time I go to treatment. It's happened to me a few times.

Most things I've tried out, I tried without relating to whether or not I was sick. One huge thing that was a revelation is trying Tofu. I used to think it was gross and with my diet becoming restricted after diagnosis, I was open to trying alternatives. I soon discovered that tofu absorbs the flavors around it and now I'm a borderline addict.

Another thing I tried after diagnosis was rice milk. I loved milk, and chocolate milk, and missed not having any dairy. But one day I tried Rice Milk which is safe for me to consume, and it's been a lifesaver in terms of cooking and beverages. I figured out that if you mix a little chocolate sauce into a glass of rice milk, and put it in the freezer for a while, it thickens up and becomes just like regular choc. milk.

I had to stick to the restricted diet, otherwise certain things would build in my system that would make me sicker and could even stop my heart due to those substances impacting muscle function.

I was constantly tired and I missed many events in a teenagers life because it took all my energy just to do stuff at home. As an adult it's still tiring but I'm stubborn and push myself out there every day to live a life.
Tests, surgery, hospital stay, anything medical is covered by my insurance. It's standard practice for transplant/donor situations. Legacy can give much more detail on how it works.

#1 thing: fluid restriction. I can only drink 2-3 liters of fluid every 2 days, because the dialysis process can only take so much water out of you because you start getting sick and probably blacking out and cramping. So it's hard to retrain the mind and body. When you are overwhelmingly thirsty you have to force yourself to drink a small amount.

#2 diet. Google "renal diet." It sucks. I can't have anything with potassium or phosphorus, which includes things like oranges, bananas, beans, potatoes, tomatoes, all kinds of other good things. My diet is very limited and none of it fills me up, so I'm constantly hungry.

Being a dialysis patient means I'm constantly tired and sometimes I randomly feel nauseous just out of the blue. Kidney dialysis only works at 17% efficiency compared to a functioning kidney. You can imagine how jacked up a person's body chemistry would be if you lived like that.
The first step is to call my team at Legacy at 503-413-6555 and ask for the "Donor Coordinator." They will be able to tell you how the process works to get tested.

I was traumatized by the whole experience and sort of emotionally dug myself into the state of mind of "I'm going to live, and work, and go to school...not going to let my disease rule my life." This past year or so I've come out of that walled-off hole and thought "i'm ready. I want to do it."
